speaker_role: former admissions officer/director at highly selective colleges (self-reported ~6% acceptance rate); now runs a paid application review service
commercial_incentive: speaker promotes his own paid application review service on his own channel and website
key_insights: Senior-year first-quarter/first-semester grade reports are sent directly from high schools to colleges and become part of the file reviewed before final decisions, so an application is not 'frozen' once submitted.
Grade reports typically go out mid-November for ED/EA applicants and around early-to-mid February for regular decision, timed to reach committees before final decisions are finalized.
Colleges evaluate grade trends (improving, stable, or declining) in the context of course rigor, the school profile, and the counselor letter, rather than judging any single grade in isolation.
A modest dip in senior grades (e.g., A to A-/B+) is generally treated differently than a large drop (e.g., A to C), especially when the student also took on harder coursework that term.
A grade drop specifically in a subject tied to the student's intended major (e.g., calculus for an engineering applicant) draws more scrutiny than a dip in an unrelated subject.

Students can proactively explain grade changes via the Common App additional information section or ask a counselor to add context in a letter or follow-up email, but over-explaining a minor dip can itself read as a red flag.

Admissions offers are effectively conditional on maintaining similar performance through both semesters of senior year; the speaker states he has personally rescinded offers over second-semester grade drops.

Students dually enrolled in college courses may need to personally request their registrar send updated grade reports directly to colleges, since this doesn't always happen automatically through the high school transcript.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker states he worked at colleges admitting about 6% of applicants, per Andrew Hoffman
First-quarter/semester grade reports are typically sent mid-November for ED/EA and early-to-mid February for regular decision, per Hoffman
Admissions committees at highly selective colleges reportedly convene final early-round decisions the first week of December, per Hoffman
notable_or_distinctive: Explains the specific mechanics and timing of the high-school-to-college grade-report pipeline (including self-reported transcript systems like STARS and the need to separately request dual-enrollment grade reports) in more procedural detail than typical general advice.
reliability_notes: Speaker's specific selectivity and rescission claims are self-reported and unverifiable; the video ends with a clear pitch for his paid application review service, a commercial incentive, though the informational content itself appears consistent with commonly published admissions practice.
